title: I saw a windfoil on TV and wanted to ride one, so I made a sailing shooter where you can't go straight into the wind
author: office-canard
selftext:
I saw windfoiling on TV and wanted to ride one. A windfoil is a windsurf board with an underwater wing. Once you're fast enough, the whole board lifts out of the water and flies.



FOIL OF THE DEAD started there, as a sailing game. The rule that shaped everything is simple: you have a sail, not an engine, so you can't go straight into the wind. Catch it from the side and you pick up speed, rise onto the foil, and fly. Point too close to it and you drop.



Then I added zombies. Shooting and staying up on the foil both depend on one thing, which way your board is pointing. Turn toward a zombie and you might turn into the wind and fall. That shared input is the whole game.



Two rules I kept coming back to:

\- An enemy that doesn't chase you basically doesn't exist.

\- Turning itself should never be the stressful part, so the board turns at the same rate in every direction.



Early on, the worst part was not knowing whether you were about to lift off or fall. Instead of changing the physics, I added a gauge that shows your angle to the wind and whether you'll fly. Just having it there took away most of the stress.



The zombies, boats and everything else in 3D are built in code, not from asset packs. I wanted a charmingly crude, B-movie comic horror look, and I wanted the zombies to have something cute about them. I rebuilt them again and again until they did.



How AI fit in: Claude wrote the code, including the sailing physics (sail force, foil lift, pumping) and those code-built zombies. Claude can't hear the game or feel it in its hands, so it measured instead: Node test harnesses, a headless browser, and an automated sailor steering the board. The feel and the look were my job, judged on a real phone.
